newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Reshuffle rumour hits S.Africa rand despite denial.
newsitem.headline: Reshuffle rumour hits S.Africa rand despite denial.

text.p: South Africa's rand started the first full trading week of the New Year in familiar terrain on Monday, coming under renewed speculative attack on market jitters about a rumoured cabinet reshuffle.

Government officials denied market talk that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel was about to be replaced by Alec Erwin from the trade and industry ministry, but dealers remained edgy after the political upheavals of 1996.

"Nothing would surprise me in South Africa, but I think it's unlikely. We've had too many finance ministers in recent years and to have yet another one would be a bad mistake," said Dennis Dykes, chief economist at Nedcor bank.
A spokesman for President Nelson Mandela reiterated there were no imminent plans for a cabinet reshuffle involving a change in finance minister.
"This is not true. There is no intention to do that on the part of the president," Parks Mankahlana told Reuters.

But the rand failed to take heart, losing further ground against a strong dollar to reach a day's low of 4.7190/7240, a loss of over two cents, before recovering slightly as the central Reserve Bank stepped in to provide liquidity.
Reshuffle talk gained momentum on Friday following newspaper reports quoting "top African National Congress (ANC) sources" as saying Mandela would announce a major change early next month.
The reports suggested that Erwin was likely to replace Manuel, although some dealers said there were also rumours that Manuel's deputy Gill Marcus might be promoted to the job.
Manuel was tipped to become foreign minister in place of Alfred Nzo.
Currency dealers said the markets might be glad to see a new face handling the country's most daunting portfolio, but renewed political uncertainty was bad for South African assets.

A February reshuffle would leave Manuel in the strange position of a finance minister who never presented a budget, a consideration which has added to scepticism about any imminent upheaval. Manuel is due to unveil his maiden budget on March 12.
Manuel, the country's first ANC finance minister, replaced the non-political Chris Liebenberg after he resigned for personal reasons last April.
Manuel's appointment failed to instill confidence in financial markets, already jittery following the first fall in the rand in February. The rand fell 29 percent against the dollar in 1996.
The minister has continued to take flak from market pundits for his supposed inexperience, although his June macro-economic strategy for growth won plaudits from business.
He has also spoken out strongly on inflation and curbing the budget deficit, warning again at the weekend that the rand would continue to weaken until inflation was firmly under control.
Trade and Industry Ministry spokesman Ismail Lagardien said reports that Erwin, who is white, would replace Manuel, who is black, were racist.
"To say we are going to replace our first black finance minister with a white minister, is overt racism."
